description: Gnomon Labs: a web app that compares south pole landing sites by Sun and Earth visibility above the horizon, to help plan power and communication windows. Built solo as a focused 48-hour MVP. Stack: TypeScript, React/Next.js, astronomy-engine and Recharts for the app, Vitest for tests, and Python with Skyfield to validate results against JPL ephemerides. The write-up will document how AI tools were used.
summary: A tool that compares south-pole lunar landing sites by Sun and Earth altitude over time, to find solar-power and direct-to-Earth communication windows.
details:
The Lunar Landing Site Navigator compares candidate lunar south-pole landing sites by how long the Sun and Earth stay above the horizon. Near the pole the Sun stays low, so solar power depends on timing and terrain, and Earth stays near the horizon, so direct communication comes and goes. The user picks up to four sites and a date range; the app computes Sun and Earth altitude every hour from each site's position on the Moon, then reports the share of time the Sun, the Earth and both are above a chosen threshold, plus the longest night. Results are shown as a ranking, altitude charts and a polar map.

Method: Sun and Earth vectors come from astronomy-engine, rotated into the Moon's body-fixed frame with the IAU rotation model. The results were checked against a reference table generated with JPL SPICE (DE440): the largest difference is 0.00115 degrees for the Sun and 0.00067 degrees for Earth, within a project tolerance of 0.005 degrees.

Impact: a quick first screening of landing sites for mission planners, with a transparent and tested method.

Limitations: the Moon is modelled as a smooth sphere, so terrain shadows and crater walls are not included. Shackleton's centre is in permanent shadow, which the model cannot show, so its Sun results are marked as a model artefact. Artemis III sites are centres of candidate regions, not exact landing points. The 0 degree power and communication thresholds are an assumption, and NASA has not confirmed the tolerance.

Tools: Next.js, TypeScript, Recharts, Vitest, astronomy-engine, Python with spiceypy for the reference table. Deployed on Vercel.

AI disclosure: AI tools (Claude and DeepSeek) helped write and review code, the validation script and this text. Each AI-assisted step is logged in the repository in notes/ai-usage-log.md, with what a person checked or changed.
projectRefs: USGS Artemis III candidate landing site navigational grids
